weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.character: IdentityAccessManagement: the per-gateway, RWMutex-guarded identity store (singleton per S3ApiServer) plus the Auth middleware wrapping every S3 route; Identity/Account/Credential value types
gotchas: scrubInternalHeaders must run before any auth path; handlers trust headers like the object-lock, version-id and SSE key-material ones, and SeaweedFSPrincipalHeader is read back by buildPrincipalARN.
isEnabled() reads isAuthEnabled without the mutex, while writers set it under iam.m; once true it is never turned off.
DeleteObjects (POST ?delete with no object) skips per-request authorization here on purpose; DeleteMultipleObjectsHandler must call AuthorizeObjectDelete per key.
ListBuckets with an empty bucket defers authorization to the handler (per-bucket filtering), except for an anonymous identity with no List action, which is denied up front.
Groups in a static config file are ignored with a warning (groups are managed via the IAM API).
${VAR} references in a static file's keys are expanded from the environment; a credential with an unset or empty variable is dropped, not loaded literally.
LookupByAccessKey returns pointers into live maps: callers must not mutate them.
A native bare Admin action survives attaching IAM policies (#11226); only an explicit Deny in an attached policy removes it.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.if_broken: Requests are wrongly denied or allowed gateway-wide; revoked keys keep working; static admin credentials can disappear on a reload; the advanced-IAM engine evaluates stale policies.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.ux: Decides between 403 AccessDenied / InvalidAccessKeyId / SignatureDoesNotMatch and success for every client; determines whether an unconfigured `docker run seaweedfs` accepts anonymous requests.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.what: Holds every identity, access key, account, policy and group the gateway knows, loaded from up to three sources: a static -config/-iam.config file (immutable 'static' identities), the credential manager store (filer/Postgres, 'dynamic'), and AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET env vars (a static admin). Replace/Merge rebuild the in-memory maps atomically; UpsertIdentity, RemoveIdentity, PutPolicy and PutGroup apply pushed single changes; UpsertIdentity re-reads the user's service accounts from the credential store, because the pushed proto carries only the user's own keys and the merge replaces the identity (#12394). Auth(handler, action) is the middleware on each route: it scrubs internal headers, authenticates by auth type (SigV2, SigV4 header/presigned/streaming, JWT via IAM integration, anonymous) and authorizes. Authorization order: Phase-1 bucket policy (explicit Deny wins; Allow bypasses IAM unless an identity, group or session policy explicitly denies), then VerifyActionPermission via one of four routes (IAM integration, attached IAM policies, legacy 'Action:bucket/prefix' strings via CanDo, or deny). Attached IAM policies are evaluated with the target from resolveS3AuthTarget, so s3vectors:* actions keep their own action and vector-bucket resource (with the vector condition keys from vectorIAMConditions, and no bucket priming), and with principal variables where an assumed-role session's aws:username and aws:userid come from the session's user claim rather than its session name (#12572). It also authorizes keys the URL does not name (copy source, DeleteObjects body keys, POST Object form key) on a synthesized request, priming the bucket first so its policy is in the engine; a bucket load that fails for a reason other than NoSuchBucket fails the request.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.when: Auth runs on every routed S3 request before the circuit breaker and handler. Config loads run at startup (file, then store with 10 retries at 2s, then env), on SIGHUP for the file, on filer metadata events via scheduleReload, every 1 min by polling for the Postgres store, and on gRPC pushes from peers (UpsertIdentity/RemoveIdentity/PutPolicy/PutGroup).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.why: Consequence: this is the S3 security perimeter; every route is wrapped in iam.Auth, so a bug here is either an outage (everyone denied) or a breach (anyone allowed). Design: static identities cannot be overwritten by dynamic store reloads, but a config-file reload is authoritative for the identities that file declares, so a key revoked by editing the file stops authenticating without a restart. Loads are serialized end to end by reloadMu so an older snapshot cannot overwrite a newer one, and failed reloads retry every 5s, coalesced through a 1-slot channel. Pointing at a config file that yields no identities enables auth and denies everyone instead of falling open. With no config at all, auth stays off ('no credentials = allow all', #9557). AWS compatibility: bucket-policy Allow can grant what identity policies omit, but never overrides an explicit identity-side Deny; listings scope by ?prefix= only for list actions so an object-scoped grant cannot authorize bucket subresources; a denied authenticated request on a malformed bucket name answers InvalidBucketName like AWS.

gotchas: A policy that already has non-blank 'content' keeps it and its 'document' is ignored; a blank 'content' counts as absent, so the document wins.
When anything is rewritten the whole file is re-encoded from a map, so key order changes; the proto parser does not care, but a diff of the normalized bytes against the file will.
A file that is not a JSON object, or whose 'policies' is not an array of objects, is passed through unchanged for the proto parser to reject.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.if_broken: Identities relying on policies from an advanced IAM file get AccessDenied, because their policies parse as empty.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.ux: Operators can use one IAM config file in either policy form; policies attached by name keep working.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.what: normalizeAdvancedIAMPolicies rewrites policies written in the advanced-IAM form {"name", "document": {...}} into the S3-config form {"name", "content": "<json string>"} before the protobuf parser sees the file. A document that is already a JSON string is used verbatim; an object is re-encoded as a string; anything it cannot rewrite is left untouched.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.when: Every static config load (loadS3ApiConfigurationFromBytes in auth_credentials.go), at startup and on SIGHUP.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.why: Consequence: with -s3.iam.config and no -s3.config, the same file is parsed as the S3 identity config; protojson silently drops the unknown 'document' field, leaving a policy with empty content that 'fails every later parse and takes the whole runtime policy sync down with it' (author comment). Design: the rewrite is all-or-nothing per policy, so a failure never strips a policy's only definition.

weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.character: S3ApiServer background loop: one long-lived filer metadata subscription per gateway that fans events out to cache and config refreshers
gotchas: The subscription is fatal-on-error per attempt and retried forever (util.RetryUntil with an always-true predicate); a broken filer means silent staleness, not a crash.
Handler errors are ignored (_ =); a failed refresh is only logged by the handler itself.
The circuit-breaker reload is triggered only for the exact file name in /etc/s3.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.if_broken: Gateways serve stale bucket configs (versioning, policies, CORS) and stale credentials (revoked keys keep working) until restart or TTL.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.ux: Bucket settings, IAM users/policies, OIDC providers and rate limits changed anywhere take effect on every gateway within moments.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.what: subscribeMetaEvents follows filer metadata events under /etc (plus BucketsPath and the IAM directories passed in by the constructor) from server start, retrying forever. For each event (handling renames as delete-from-old-dir plus create-in-new-dir) it calls: onBucketMetadataChange (bucket created/updated/deleted under BucketsPath → owner index maintenance, bucket-policy mirror into advanced IAM, BucketRegistry refresh/eviction, bucket config cache refresh of resident entries or invalidation), onIamConfigChange (identity file or identities/policies/service_accounts/groups dirs → coalesced IAM reload), onOIDCProviderChange (refresh OIDC providers from the store), onRoleChange (invalidate the role cache, honoring a custom role-store directory) and onCircuitBreakerConfigChange (/etc/s3/circuit_breaker.json → reload limits, reset on delete).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.when: Started as a goroutine at the end of NewS3ApiServerWithStore and runs for the life of the process; each filer metadata event is processed synchronously, in order.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.why: Consequence: this is what keeps every gateway's caches and IAM state consistent with changes made through any other gateway, the admin UI or weed shell; without it, bucket config would only refresh at the 60-minute cache TTL and IAM changes would need a restart. Design: config-cache updates only refresh buckets already resident (never warm the cache from events) and drop negative entries so a newly created bucket is visible at once; IAM changes schedule a coalesced full reload instead of applying partial diffs, so a burst of edits costs one reload.

weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.character: One IdentityAccessManagement method: a thin delegate to the advanced IAM integration
gotchas: Without advanced IAM every trust check fails, so AssumeRole cannot succeed in a legacy-identities-only deployment.

s3_iam_middleware.go declares the same method on its integration interface and implements it by calling the IAM manager; this file is the IdentityAccessManagement-side delegate that s3api_sts.go calls.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.if_broken: Role assumption either always fails or ignores trust policies (privilege escalation).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.ux: AccessDenied from AssumeRole when the role's trust policy does not name the caller.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.what: ValidateTrustPolicyForPrincipal(roleArn, principalArn) asks the IAM integration whether the role's trust policy lets that principal assume it, and fails with 'IAM integration not available' when there is none.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.when: STS AssumeRole (the caller's principal ARN) and AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity (the LDAP user's principal ARN) in s3api_sts.go, before any credentials are minted.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.why: Consequence: AssumeRole must check the target role's trust policy; without it any authenticated user could assume any role. Design: the trust evaluation lives in the advanced IAM manager (weed/iam), so the legacy identity store only forwards; failing closed when no integration exists means STS cannot grant roles without the engine that defines them.

weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.character: IdentityAccessManagement methods plus stateless helpers implementing legacy AWS Signature Version 2 (header, presigned query, POST policy); derived from MinIO
gotchas: Presigned V2 URLs have no maximum lifetime (SigV4 caps at 7 days).
When x-amz-date is present, the Date line in the string-to-sign is blanked (it is covered through the x-amz-* headers instead).
The invalid-access-key warnings log the full attempted access key id.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.if_broken: Legacy clients are locked out, or forged V2 requests are accepted.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.issue_note: Header-signed SigV2 requests are never checked for freshness: doesSignV2Match verifies the HMAC over the Date header but never compares that date to the server clock (the only RequestTimeTooSkewed check in the package is in the SigV4 header path). A captured V2-signed request can therefore be replayed indefinitely until the key is rotated, where AWS rejects V2 requests more than 15 minutes old. Reproduced at b9866bae (a header-signed request dated a year ago was accepted); doesSignV2Match is unchanged at 917cf534. The second half of the earlier flag, subresources missing from resourceList so that a signature for GET /bucket also authenticated ?cors, ?tagging, ?object-lock or ?encryption, is fixed upstream by #12575 (917cf534).
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.ux: Legacy V2 clients authenticate; failures answer SignatureDoesNotMatch / InvalidAccessKeyId / AccessDenied (expired presign).
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.what: Verifies 'Authorization: AWS <key>:<sig>' requests, presigned ?AWSAccessKeyId&Expires&Signature URLs and V2 POST-policy forms: looks up the key, rejects expired credentials, rebuilds the V2 string-to-sign (method, Content-MD5, Content-Type, Date or Expires, sorted x-amz-* headers, path plus the subresources in resourceList), computes HMAC-SHA1 and compares in constant time after base64-decoding both sides; records the access key id for audit. resourceList holds every query key that selects an operation (acl, cors, tagging, object-lock, retention, legal-hold, encryption, publicAccessBlock, replication, seaweedfs-quota and the rest), and every value of a repeated key is signed. After a header or presigned V2 match, the request body is bound with bindSignedPayload as unsigned payload, so only Content-MD5 is checked against it.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.when: authenticateRequestInternal for authTypeSignedV2 / authTypePresignedV2; doesPolicySignatureV2Match from the POST Object handler.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.why: Consequence: older SDKs and tools (s3cmd defaults, legacy apps) still sign with V2; without this they cannot talk to the gateway. Design: constant-time comparison avoids a signature timing oracle; presigned expiry is checked before the key lookup. Every operation-selecting subresource is in the canonical resource because a signature covering only the path would authorize the other operations on it (#12575); repeated keys are all signed because handlers read the first value. AWS compatibility: the V2 spec's canonical resource, plus SeaweedFS's own seaweedfs-quota and renameObject subresources.

weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.character: IdentityAccessManagement methods plus stateless helpers implementing AWS Signature Version 4 verification (header, presigned query and POST-policy forms); derived from MinIO's implementation
gotchas: A Credential scope date that does not parse returns ErrMalformedCredentialDate, which has no s3err mapping and panics the error writer (see the s3err/ issue note).
Presigned requests check only expiry, not a future X-Amz-Date: ErrRequestNotReadyYet is never used, so a key holder can date a URL in the future and keep it valid well past 7 days from now.
X-Forwarded-Host/Port/Proto are tried as host candidates from any client (not only trusted proxies); this only changes which host the signature must cover, so it is not a bypass.
doesSignatureMatch and doesPresignedSignatureMatch are identical wrappers over verifyV4Signature(r, false).
The invalid-access-key warning logs the full attempted access key id.
Streaming payloads (STREAMING-*) are not bound here; their bodies are checked chunk by chunk in chunked_reader_v4.go, which does not enforce the trailer-mode signatures (see that node).
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.if_broken: All SigV4 clients fail, or forged / replayed requests are accepted.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.ux: SignatureDoesNotMatch, RequestTimeTooSkewed, AccessDenied (expired presign), InvalidAccessKeyId, ExpiredToken for clients; presigned URLs work behind reverse proxies when -s3.externalUrl or forwarded headers are set.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.what: verifyV4Signature: extract auth info (Credential scope, SignedHeaders, Signature, date) from the Authorization header or the X-Amz-* query → look up the access key (static identity) or, if absent and a session token is present, validate the STS session through the IAM integration → check presigned expiry → require every x-amz-* request header to be signed (verifySignedHeadersCoverage) → build the canonical request and recompute the HMAC chain, trying several host candidates (configured external host, X-Forwarded-Host/Port/Proto variants, Host) and path forms (original pre-rewrite path, escaped, decoded, and X-Forwarded-Prefix variants from trusted proxies only) → constant-time compare. Then it records the access key id in the context, and denies when a virtual-host-signed bucket differs from the routed bucket. reqSignatureV4Verify then binds the body to the signed payload hash (bindSignedPayload in request_body.go). Also validateSTSSessionToken (key id, expiry, non-empty principal; Iceberg-vended sessions must still be backed by a live, unchanged stored key; aws:username is the session's ExternalUserId, never a forwarded claim) and doesPolicySignatureV4Match for POST Object.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.when: authenticateRequestInternal (auth_credentials.go) for SigV4 header, presigned and signed-streaming requests (the streaming chunk signatures are then checked in chunked_reader_v4.go); doesPolicySignatureV4Match from the POST Object handler.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.why: Consequence: SigV4 is how nearly every SDK authenticates; an error here either locks out all clients or accepts forged requests. Design: real deployments sit behind proxies and ingresses that rewrite Host, port or path, so several host and path forms are tried; only X-Forwarded-Prefix is gated on trusted proxies, because it changes which path the signature covers. The virtual-host bucket check stops a request signed for bucket A on a.example.com from being routed to bucket B. Unsigned x-amz-* headers are rejected because handlers act on them (SSE, ACL, lock headers), except the presign protocol parameters and SSE-C key headers, which AWS SDKs leave unsigned on presigned URLs. A session token on a request signed by a static key is tolerated but ignored (some credential vendors, such as Unity Catalog, emit one with static keys). AWS compatibility: 15-minute clock-skew limit for header auth, 7-day (604800s) maximum presign expiry, non-s3 services (IAM/STS POSTs) have their body hashed up to a 10 MiB limit when no payload hash is sent.

weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.character: BucketRegistry: a second per-gateway bucket cache (LRU of BucketMetaData plus an LRU 'not found' set, with singleflight loading) focused on ownership and ACL; one instance per S3ApiServer
gotchas: The not-found set has no TTL: a bucket stays NoSuchBucket here until a metadata event (LoadBucketMetadata / RemoveBucketMetadata) or LRU eviction clears it; unlike BucketConfigCache's negative entries (ttl/4, at least 30s).
LoadBucketMetadata only refreshes buckets already in the cache; it never adds new ones.

Bucket ownership, owner and ACL are parsed from the same Extended keys here AND in newBucketConfigFromEntry (s3api_bucket_config.go), into two different caches with slightly different shapes (effective vs raw ownership); a change to one parse does not reach the other.
buildBucketMetadata JSON-marshals the whole (cipher-key-scrubbed) entry on every build, only for a debug log line.
loadBucketMetadataFromFiler is a package var so tests can stub the filer read.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.if_broken: Objects get the uploader instead of the bucket owner as owner (or vice versa), ACL-based access breaks, and table-bucket layout rules stop applying.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.ux: Invisible; it decides the Owner shown in listings and ACLs, and whether BucketOwnerEnforced takes effect.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.what: Caches, per bucket: whether it is an S3 Tables bucket, its effective ObjectOwnership (absent/invalid → BucketOwnerEnforced), its owner (account id from the owner key, else resolved from the creating identity name, else admin) and parsed ACL grants. GetBucketMetadata serves from cache, answers NoSuchBucket from the not-found set, or loads from the filer once per bucket even under concurrent misses (singleflight). LoadBucketMetadata/RemoveBucketMetadata are called by the metadata subscription to refresh or evict entries. bucketOwnerAccountId is shared with s3api_bucket_config.go.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.when: On object writes (owner stamping), ACL handlers, table-bucket checks (bucket_paths.go), and on every bucket create/update/delete event from the filer metadata subscription.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.why: Consequence: PutObject's object-owner decision (setObjectOwnerFromRequest), ACL checks and isTableBucket all ask this registry; a wrong answer makes objects owned by the wrong account or lets plain-object rules apply to a table bucket. Design: singleflight stops a thundering herd of filer lookups for a cold bucket; the cache is capped at bucketCacheCapacity (65536) so huge deployments keep only the hot set; owners recorded outside the S3 API (admin UI, weed shell) name an identity, which is resolved to its account here.

weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.character: S3ApiServer methods plus stateless package-level validators; one compiled regexp and two swappable package vars (clock, lookup) used as test seams
gotchas: bucketRoot ignores its bucket argument: all bucket types share option.BucketsPath.

isTableBucket fails open: any registry/filer error other than not-found is logged at V(1) and answered 'not a table bucket', so during a transient error a table bucket gets plain-bucket rules for the layout check.
Only PUT, GET, HEAD, DELETE and DeleteObjects accept the verify key; multipart, copy, rename, ACL, tagging and POST policy still apply the plain layout rule (author comment).
volumeVerifyNow and volumeVerifyLookup are package vars so tests can swap the clock and the lookup; read them at call time, never cache them.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.if_broken: A wrong bucketDir puts every object in, or reads it from, the wrong filer directory. isTableBucket returning true for a plain bucket rejects nearly every key; returning false for a table bucket lets arbitrary objects into it. A loosened verify-key check turns the exception into a way to store arbitrary data in table buckets.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.ux: Invisible for plain buckets. On a table bucket a client writing outside the Iceberg layout gets an InvalidIcebergLayout error, while Snowflake's volume verification succeeds.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.what: Says where a bucket lives in the filer (bucketDir = BucketsPath/<bucket>, bucketPrefix, getBucketEntry, bucketExists) and enforces the S3 Tables object layout: in a table bucket an object must sit under namespace/table/{data|metadata}/… or be a table marker file at namespace/table/<marker>. It also carves out one narrow exception, the Snowflake external-volume verification key verify_<13-digit epoch ms>_<n> at the bucket root. collectionForCopyPath gives a server-side copy the destination bucket's collection when a filer group is set (the group-prefixed name from getCollectionName), so copied chunks are not left to the filer's path-rule precedence (#12499).
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.when: getBucketEntry/bucketExists run for bucket-scoped requests and config loads; validateTableBucketObjectPath(OrVerify) runs inside object read/write handlers for every key of a table bucket; volumeVerifyPutAllowed gates the PUT handler only when the key matched the verify shape.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.why: Consequence: every handler builds filer paths through bucketDir/bucketPrefix, so this decides where every object is read and written; getBucketEntry refuses dot-prefixed names so internal trees under /buckets (.system) can never be addressed as a bucket. Design: isTableBucket asks the in-memory bucketRegistry first and only falls back to a filer lookup when there is no registry. AWS/ecosystem compatibility: Snowflake's SYSTEM$VERIFY_EXTERNAL_VOLUME writes, reads, lists and deletes a 21-byte verify_… object at the volume root before using it; without the exception a table bucket cannot be a Snowflake external volume. The exception is fenced so it cannot store data: bucket root only, one regex shape, never a directory, PUT dated within ±1h of the server clock, Content-Length ≤ 1024 with no chunked/undeclared body, no user metadata, tagging, stored content headers or zip extraction.

weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.character: The leader-elected background loop that publishes bucket size metrics and enforces bucket quotas by flipping buckets read-only
gotchas: Enforcement lags by up to a minute plus vacuum, so a bucket can overshoot its quota by a minute of writes.
Every gateway uses the same lock owner string (<filer>-s3-metrics), so log lines about the owner cannot tell gateways apart; the renew token still keeps only one holder.
Without -master the loop silently does nothing, so quotas are never enforced.
The lock goes through Filers[0] only; if that filer is down no gateway collects metrics or enforces quotas.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.if_broken: Quotas stop being enforced (or never lift), and size dashboards go stale.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.ux: Prometheus shows per-bucket size; a bucket at quota starts refusing writes shortly after crossing it and accepts them again after deletes and vacuum.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.what: startBucketSizeMetricsLoop waits 10s, then holds a long-lived distributed lock 's3.leader' through the first filer. Every minute, while it holds the lock, it asks a master for CollectionStatistics, lists the buckets, sets each bucket's logical size, physical size and object-count gauges, and calls enforceBucketQuotas. That function reads filer.conf, flips each bucket's read-only flag to match LogicalSize() against its quota (ApplyBucketQuotaReadOnly) and saves filer.conf only when a flag changed.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.when: Started from the server constructor as a goroutine; runs every minute for the life of the process, only on the gateway holding the lock.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.why: Consequence: quotas are enforced here, not on the write path: a bucket over quota becomes read-only within about a minute, and a bucket under quota is writable again. Design: the master summarises collection statistics so the gateway does not pull every volume each minute. The leader lock keeps several gateways from rewriting filer.conf at once. LogicalSize subtracts un-vacuumed deleted bytes so vacuum lag never counts against a bucket, matching the Admin UI.

weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.character: s3ChunkedReader: a per-request io.ReadCloser state machine that decodes aws-chunked upload bodies (derived from MinIO), plus the ChecksumAlgorithm enum and hash constructors used across the write path
gotchas: If several x-amz-checksum-* lines appear in the trailer, the last one wins.
Close() is a no-op; the caller closes the underlying body.
ChecksumAlgorithm/getCheckSumWriter defined here are also used by putToFiler and multipart checksum computation.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.if_broken: Objects are stored with framing garbage, uploads fail for modern SDKs, or tampered bodies are accepted.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.issue_note: For STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD-TRAILER uploads the body is not authenticated. Chunk signatures are only checked when a chunk line carries ';chunk-signature=' (an absent signature is simply skipped), and in trailer mode the final chunk goes straight to the trailer checksum, so neither the last chunk signature nor x-amz-trailer-signature is ever verified. Reproduced against this commit with a throwaway test: a reader built as newChunkedReader builds it with auth on (credential set, hasTrailer) returned an attacker-chosen body without error when the chunks carried no signatures and the trailer carried a matching CRC32. The header (seed) signature still has to be valid, so this is a body-integrity gap (replay of captured headers within the 15-minute window, or MITM on plain HTTP), not an authentication bypass. Without a trailer, a missing final-chunk signature does fail.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.ux: Streaming uploads from modern SDKs work; corrupt or tampered chunks fail with chunk-signature / checksum mismatch errors.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.what: newChunkedReader verifies the request's SigV4 header signature (the seed signature) for signed streaming uploads and returns a reader that strips the aws-chunked framing ('<hex size>;chunk-signature=<sig>\r\n<data>\r\n'), recomputes each chunk's signature as an HMAC chained from the previous one, hashes the payload with the advertised trailer checksum (CRC32, CRC32C, CRC64NVME, SHA1, SHA256), and checks the trailer 'x-amz-checksum-*' line against it. It also handles STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER (no chunk signatures, checksum only). Chunk header lines are capped at 4 KiB.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.when: getRequestDataReader (s3api_put_object_helper.go) for PUT / UploadPart bodies whose x-amz-content-sha256 is a STREAMING-* value.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.why: Consequence: SDKs upload large or streaming bodies (aws-cli, boto3, Java SDK v2 with checksums) in aws-chunked framing; without this decoder the stored object would contain the framing bytes. Design: chained chunk signatures are what authenticate the BODY of a streaming SigV4 upload, since the header signature covers only the literal STREAMING-... payload marker; trailer checksums give end-to-end integrity for unsigned streaming. AWS compatibility: the signed, signed-trailer and unsigned-trailer streaming variants and the five flexible checksum algorithms.

weed/s3api/cors/.character: The CORS engine as a package of its own: the bucket CORSConfiguration types, their validation, rule matching, and the middleware that answers preflights and decorates responses
gotchas: The response always echoes the request Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, even for a '*' rule (AWS answers '*' without credentials).
A preflight whose method or headers are not allowed still gets 200 with Allow-Origin but no Allow-Methods; the browser blocks it, but it is not the 403 AWS sends.
Non-preflight requests are served even when no rule matches; only the CORS headers are withheld, and the browser hides the response.
weed/s3api/cors/.if_broken: Browser uploads and downloads fail with CORS errors, or responses become readable from origins the bucket owner never allowed.
weed/s3api/cors/.issue_note: EvaluateRequest stops at the first rule whose AllowedOrigins match, and for a preflight it builds the response from that rule even when its AllowedMethods (or AllowedHeaders) do not cover the request. AWS picks the first rule that matches origin AND method AND headers. A common configuration therefore fails: rule 1 {origins:[*], methods:[GET]}, rule 2 {origins:[https://app.example.com], methods:[PUT,POST]}. Probe (cors package test): a PUT preflight from https://app.example.com → allowOrigin set, allowMethods "" (browser blocks the upload); the actual PUT request evaluated without a preflight → allowMethods "PUT, POST". Only the actual-request path checks the method before accepting a rule.
weed/s3api/cors/.ux: Browsers get Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers/Expose-Headers/Max-Age as configured; a disallowed preflight fails in the browser console.
weed/s3api/cors/.what: cors.go defines CORSRule / CORSConfiguration (XML and JSON), ValidateConfiguration (1–100 rules; methods limited to GET/PUT/POST/DELETE/HEAD; at most one origin wildcard, only after http:// or https://), ParseRequest, EvaluateRequest (first rule whose origin matches; for actual requests the method must match too), the preflight and actual response builders, and ApplyHeaders. middleware.go wraps every request. It reads the bucket's CORS configuration through an interface, falls back to a global configuration when the bucket has none or does not exist, adds 'Vary: Origin', answers OPTIONS preflights itself (403 when nothing matches), and lets non-preflight requests through even when no rule matches.
weed/s3api/cors/.when: Every S3 request through the router-level middleware and every OPTIONS preflight; ValidateConfiguration on PutBucketCors.
weed/s3api/cors/.why: Consequence: browsers block every cross-origin upload or download that does not get the right Access-Control-* headers, so web apps that talk to S3 directly depend on this. Design: the engine sits behind small interfaces (BucketChecker, CORSConfigGetter) so it does not import the gateway, and a missing bucket falls back to the global configuration instead of a 403, so a preflight cannot reveal whether a bucket exists. AWS compatibility: rule shape, validation limits and wildcard rules follow PutBucketCors. Expose '*' is expanded to the standard S3 headers because browsers treat '*' literally on credentialed requests.

weed/s3api/crc_combine.go.character: CRC combination math: the CRC of a concatenation from the CRCs of its parts, for CRC32, CRC32C and CRC64NVME
gotchas: Each call rebuilds the zero operators; cost is O(log len2) matrix squarings per part, fine for 10,000 parts but not free.
Only fully reflected or fully unreflected CRCs are supported; anything else panics.
weed/s3api/crc_combine.go.if_broken: Completion reports a checksum that does not match the data, and SDK integrity checks fail.
weed/s3api/crc_combine.go.ux: Clients that upload multipart with CRC64NVME or full-object CRC32/CRC32C get a checksum that matches a local whole-file CRC.
weed/s3api/crc_combine.go.what: crcCombineParams holds the Rocksoft parameters for the three algorithms. combineCRC (a port of Mark Adler's crccomb.c via crc-fast-rust) applies len2 zero bytes to crc1 with GF(2) matrix squaring (gf2MatrixTimes, gf2MatrixSquare) and XORs in crc2; reflectPoly and bitReverse prepare the reflected polynomial. It panics on an unsupported reflection combination.
weed/s3api/crc_combine.go.when: computeFullObjectChecksum in filer_multipart.go, at CompleteMultipartUpload for uploads that requested a FULL_OBJECT checksum type.
weed/s3api/crc_combine.go.why: Consequence: a FULL_OBJECT checksum for a multipart object must equal the CRC of the whole object, and recomputing it would mean re-reading every byte at completion. Design: combining the per-part CRCs needs only each part's CRC and length, so CompleteMultipartUpload stays O(parts). AWS compatibility: CRC64NVME only exists as a full-object checksum on AWS, so supporting it requires this combination.

weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.character: Single stateless exported mapping function shared with weed/iamapi
gotchas: Any new permanent credential error (e.g. a duplicate policy) must be added here, or it surfaces as ServiceFailure (HTTP 500).
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.if_broken: IAM tooling misreads failures (retries forever on a missing user, or treats a duplicate as a server error).
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.ux: IAM clients get EntityAlreadyExists / NoSuchEntity instead of a generic failure, so idempotent tooling works.
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.what: CredentialErrToIamErrCode maps credential-store errors to IAM error codes: ErrUserAlreadyExists → EntityAlreadyExists, ErrUserNotFound / ErrAccessKeyNotFound → NoSuchEntity, anything else → ServiceFailure.
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.when: Embedded IAM API handlers (s3api_embedded_iam.go) and weed/iamapi management handlers, whenever a credential-manager call fails.
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.why: Consequence: IAM clients (aws iam ..., Terraform) branch on these codes; without the mapping every store error would look like a 500, or worse, a store failure could be reported as a 200. Design: one function shared by the standalone IAM server (weed/iamapi) and the embedded IAM API, so the two report identical error granularity. AWS compatibility: the codes are the AWS IAM exception names.

weed/s3api/custom_types.go.character: A single result struct for the conditional-header checks (If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since)
gotchas: Entry is nil both when the object does not exist and when the check did not need to fetch it; callers must not read nil as 'absent'.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.if_broken: Conditional requests answer from a stale or missing entry: wrong 304/412 decisions, or delete-marker 404s without their headers.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.ux: Invisible: it decides whether a client gets 200, 304 or 412.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.what: Defines ConditionalHeaderResult: the S3 error code the check decided, the object's ETag (for a 304), the entry it fetched while checking (so the handler does not look it up again) and, when the resolved key is a delete marker, that marker's entry so a missing-key answer can still carry its headers.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.when: Returned by the conditional-header evaluators the object read and write handlers call before streaming or writing.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.why: Consequence: GET, HEAD, PUT and CopyObject all evaluate conditions before acting. Returning the fetched entry saves a second filer lookup, and that lookup could see a different version than the one the condition was checked against. AWS compatibility: a 404 on a delete marker must still return x-amz-delete-marker and the version ID, which is why the marker is carried through.

weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.character: S3ApiServer methods implementing multipart upload storage on the filer: create, complete, abort, list uploads and parts, plus the ETag/checksum math
gotchas: Completion copies ALL Extended keys of the upload entry onto the object (except the key marker), so whatever createMultipartUpload stores (including object-lock fields; see the s3api_object_handlers_multipart.go issue) ends up on the object.
SSE-S3 per-chunk IVs are derived from each chunk's PART-local offset with no part term, mirroring putToFiler's partOffset=0 (see the s3api_put_handlers.go issue about keystream reuse).
Duplicate uploads of the same part number are resolved by the newest first-chunk ModifiedTsNs; the losers are deleted after commit.
listMultipartUploads lists the whole .uploads folder (math.MaxInt32 limit) on every call and keeps only a heap of the page.
The non-versioned path marks the object SeaweedFSExpiresS3 when any part carried a TTL.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.if_broken: Completed objects with missing or misordered bytes, wrong ETags that break SDK verification, orphaned part data, or chunks freed under a live object.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.issue_note: completeMultipartUpload builds the final entry three times with near-identical decorate closures (versioned decorateVersionEntry, suspended, non-versioned): upload id, parts count, part boundaries, owner, copying the upload entry's Extended, first-part SSE headers, SSE-S3 headers, ETag, checksum, mime, size. A fix to what a completed object carries must be made in all three.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.ux: Large-object uploads complete with AWS-compatible ETags and checksums; retries of Complete are safe; aborts free storage.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.what: createMultipartUpload makes <bucket>/.uploads/<uploadId> (id = sha1(key)_<uuid hex>) holding the key, owner, user metadata, ACL, checksum algorithm/type, object-lock metadata and the multipart encryption config (SSE-KMS key id/context/base IV, or SSE-S3 shared DEK + base IV, chosen from headers or the bucket default). completeMultipartUpload validates part order, ETags and sizes (non-last parts ≥5 MiB), stitches part chunks into one chunk list with rebased offsets (backfilling SSE-S3 per-chunk IVs when missing), records part boundaries and parts count, computes the multipart ETag md5(concat(part md5s))-N and COMPOSITE or FULL_OBJECT checksums (CRC combine), manifestizes chunks, and commits by versioning state: a new version under .versions/ (routed finalize transaction or mkFile + pointer update), a 'null' object for suspended buckets, or a plain object, each removing the upload dir in the same transaction when routed. A retried Complete after a commit is answered from the stored object (committedCompletion: the key's current object carries this SeaweedFSUploadId), and so is the attempt itself when its finalize reports failure after the entry was in fact committed (#12416); if the committed chunks are not this attempt's, cleanup keeps every part's data. abortMultipartUpload deletes the upload dir under the object lock, keeping chunks if the upload was in fact completed; the routed delete locks the same path a routed completion commits (uploadCommitPath: the object path in a versioned bucket, else the entry the completion writes, which for a trailing-slash key lies inside the directory), so abort and complete serialize (#12558). listMultipartUploads keeps a bounded heap of the next page; listObjectParts pages part files.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.when: CreateMultipartUpload, CompleteMultipartUpload, AbortMultipartUpload, ListParts, ListMultipartUploads (via s3api_object_handlers_multipart.go); routedUploadRemoval/writeMultipartObject from s3api_object_routed_write.go.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.why: Consequence: this is where large objects become real objects; a bug corrupts or loses large uploads, or deletes chunks still referenced by a completed object. Design: abort checks whether the upload was already completed (an object or version carrying its upload id) and then removes only metadata, because the completed object shares the part chunks; the routed abort uses an IF_EXTENDED_NOT_EQUAL condition on the object for the same reason. Completion is idempotent so SDK retries after a lost response succeed instead of answering NoSuchUpload. Manifest chunks folded during completion are tracked so they are deleted on failure and kept on success. AWS compatibility: multipart ETag format '<md5>-<parts>', InvalidPartOrder, EntityTooSmall, InvalidPart, COMPOSITE vs FULL_OBJECT checksum types (CRC64NVME full-object only; SHA1/SHA256 composite only).

weed/s3api/filer_util.go.character: S3ApiServer methods: the gateway's basic filer CRUD vocabulary (mkdir/mkFile/list/rm/getEntry/updateEntry), with stateless retry helpers
gotchas: Most helpers use context.Background(); only rm/rmObject take a ctx (consumed by retryFilerOp and the DeleteEntry RPC).
listRetry may re-deliver entries a failed attempt already saw: a doList that accumulates must reset its slice first (listWithRetry does; routed_read's listing resets explicitly).
isReservedDirectoryName names are never turned into prefix objects by mkFile.
clearDirectoryMarkerMetadata keeps only xattr-* and SeaweedFS-internal extended keys and drops the prefix-object flag; anything else stored on the marker is lost when it is demoted.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.if_broken: Retrying non-transient list errors would add latency to every miss; not retrying deletes resurfaces flaky 500s; a broken prefix-object path makes PutObject on a key that already has children fail with 'existing is directory'.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.ux: Invisible. It is why a transient filer hiccup does not show up as InternalError on deletes and listings, and why keys like 'photos' and 'photos/1.jpg' can coexist.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.what: Wraps filer_pb calls into the small set of operations handlers use: mkdir, mkdirExclusive (never replaces an existing entry), mkFile (retries as a 'prefix object' on the directory when other keys are nested under the name), list with bounded retries, rm/rmObject with idempotent-delete retries, exists, getEntry, updateEntry, getCollectionName (FilerGroup_bucket) and objectKey. rmObject turns a non-empty explicit directory marker into a plain implicit directory instead of failing.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.when: Called by nearly every handler and background loop for raw filer access; list() backs bucket and object listings, rm/rmObject back DeleteObject(s) and DeleteBucket, mkdirExclusive backs PutBucket.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.why: Design: listings retry up to 3 times (100ms then 200ms backoff) only on transient gRPC statuses, never on not-found, because a listing has no side effects and collects into a fresh slice per attempt. Deletes retry because the filer answers 'already gone' with an empty error, so a dropped reply can be re-sent safely; otherwise a lost reply would become a 500 on DeleteBucket or a per-key InternalError inside a DeleteObjects 200, which no SDK retries. mkdirExclusive exists so PutBucket cannot replace a table bucket created in its check-to-create window. AWS compatibility: S3 allows both 'a' and 'a/b' as keys; the filer cannot have a file and a directory with one name, so mkFile marks the directory itself as the object (MarkPrefixObject), and deleting such a directory key strips its object metadata (demoteDirectoryMarkerToImplicitDirectory) while keeping xattr-* and internal keys.

weed/s3api/filer_util_tags.go.character: Low-level read/replace/remove of the X-Amz-Tagging-* xattrs on an entry
gotchas: setTags and rmTags do a lookup then an unconditional whole-entry UpdateEntry, so a concurrent metadata change on the same entry can be overwritten.
weed/s3api/filer_util_tags.go.if_broken: Tags are lost or merged instead of replaced.
weed/s3api/filer_util_tags.go.issue_note: getTags has no callers anywhere in the repository, tests included; tag reads go through the entries the handlers already loaded. setTags and rmTags in the same file are live.
weed/s3api/filer_util_tags.go.what: S3TAG_PREFIX is 'X-Amz-Tagging-'. setTags looks the entry up on the given owner filer, drops every tag xattr, writes the new set and calls UpdateEntry. rmTags removes all tag xattrs, skipping the write when there were none. getTags reads them through the default filer client.
weed/s3api/filer_util_tags.go.why: Consequence: tags are stored as individual xattrs next to the object's other metadata, so replacing them must not touch anything else. Design: writes go to the key's owner filer so they serialize with routed PUTs and are visible to routed reads.

weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_helpers.go.character: Commit plumbing shared by table creates, commits and create-on-commit: exclusive, token-tagged staging of metadata files, the refusal test that decides when a staged file may go, the create-on-commit finalizer, request-size fitting, s3tables error classification and the pre-write authorization gates
gotchas: Once fitUpdateTableRequest drops FullMetadata, the table is served from its metadata file alone, so losing that file shows the table as empty.
isS3TablesNotFound matches 'not found' anywhere in the error text; isS3TablesAlreadyExists reads the message only for an untyped error.
The table commit path stages with stageCommitMetadata but still deletes by name through deleteMetadataFile, without registrationRefused or the token (see the defect on handlers_commit.go).
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_helpers.go.if_broken: Concurrent creators overwrite or delete each other's metadata, a create that failed ambiguously leaves its table pointing at a deleted file, or large commits are refused.
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_helpers.go.ux: Large tables can still commit; read-only callers cannot make the server write files under a table; the loser of a concurrent create gets 409 and the winner's table stays readable.
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_helpers.go.what: stageCommitMetadata and stageOwnedMetadata write a metadata file exclusively, tagged with a per-request token (stageTokenKey), and fall back to v{N}-<uuid>.metadata.json when the v{N} name is taken. discardStagedMetadata removes a staged file only while it still carries that token (deleteStagedMetadataFile in metadata_files.go), so a file that took the path since is kept. registrationRefused decides whether a failed registration may discard the file: a name already taken, a conflict over a still-hidden record and any other 4xx are refusals; a conflict over a record that was already published (IsPublishedTableChanged), a 5xx and a transport error are not, because the record may point at the file. finalizeCreateOnCommit applies the commit's updates to the staged template (or placeholder) metadata, stages v{N}.metadata.json the same way, registers the table with CreateTable, discards the file only when the registration was refused, and answers 409 CommitFailedException 'created concurrently' for a conflict, an existing name, or a CreateTable that answers with another table's location; on success it deletes the stage-create markers. fitUpdateTableRequest drops FullMetadata (setting ClearFullMetadata) when the request would exceed s3tables.MaxRequestBodySize. authorizeCommit (which also applies the vector namespace fence) and authorizeViewCommit ask s3tables whether the caller may update before any file is written. isS3TablesConflict and isS3TablesAlreadyExists classify a typed error by its code; isS3TablesNotFound also matches the message text.
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_helpers.go.when: Every table create (handlers_table.go), commit (handlers_commit.go) and transaction commit (handlers_transaction.go).
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_helpers.go.why: Consequence: the staging and cleanup decisions here decide whether a lost race leaves an orphan file (harmless) or deletes the file a live table points at (unreadable table). Design: the catalog pointer, not the file name, decides which writer won, so a taken name falls back to a unique one instead of failing; a staged file is deleted only after a definite refusal and only while it still carries this request's token, because an ambiguous failure may have published a record that points at it and a later create may have reused the path; authorization runs before staging because both paths write into the table directory before the catalog decides. Compatibility: 409 CommitFailedException is the retry signal for create-on-commit races.

weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_updates.go.character: Handles the set-statistics / remove-statistics commit updates that iceberg-go cannot decode, by splitting them out and patching the metadata JSON
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_updates.go.if_broken: Commits with statistics fail with 400, or statistics are lost.
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_updates.go.what: parseCommitUpdates separates set-statistics and remove-statistics actions from the other updates (which go to iceberg-go's table.Updates). set-statistics accepts either a nested statistics object or the flat fields (snapshot-id, statistics-path, file-size-in-bytes, file-footer-size-in-bytes required). applyStatisticsUpdates patches the metadata's 'statistics' array, one entry per snapshot id, keeping the first-seen order, replacing on set and dropping on remove.
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_updates.go.when: Every table and transaction commit that carries statistics updates.
weed/s3api/iceberg/commit_updates.go.why: Consequence: engines that compute table statistics (Puffin files, e.g. Trino ANALYZE or Spark) send these updates in ordinary commits; rejecting them fails the whole commit. Design: iceberg-go's MetadataBuilder has no statistics support, so the server applies them to the serialized JSON and re-parses it.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.character: POST .../tables/{table}: the Iceberg commit protocol — validate requirements, apply updates to the current metadata, stage v{N+1}.metadata.json and flip the catalog pointer with a version-token compare, retrying on conflicts
gotchas: On an UpdateTable failure that is not a conflict (a 5xx or transport error), the staged file is deleted even though the record may already point at it (see issue note).
A record without a table UUID gets a random one per request (generatedLegacyUUID) unless the metadata file carries one.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.if_broken: Commits are lost, duplicated, or leave the table pointing at a deleted metadata file.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.issue_note: When UpdateTable fails with anything other than a conflict (a 5xx, a transport error, a lost response), handleUpdateTable deletes the metadata file it staged, although the record may already point at it. A table whose record keeps only a location (fitUpdateTableRequest dropped FullMetadata for a large commit) is then served from a missing file, which buildLoadTableResult turns into empty placeholder metadata: the table appears to have no snapshots and the next commit builds on that. Reproduced at b9866bae (filer hook that applies the UpdateEntry and then answers Unavailable): the commit answers 500, the record points at v2.metadata.json and only v1.metadata.json is left on disk. The client gets a plain 500, not the spec's CommitStateUnknownException.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.ux: Concurrent writers retry on 409 instead of overwriting each other.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.what: handleUpdateTable decodes the request, normalizes requirements and splits out statistics updates (commit_updates.go). If the table does not exist, a commit with assert-create (or a staged template from the stage-create marker that matches the UUID the commit assigns) creates it through finalizeCreateOnCommit, after the CreateTable permission check that also refuses a location another record owns. Otherwise it checks the UpdateTable permission (authorizeCommit), loads the current metadata (record copy or file), validates every requirement against it, repairs foreign manifests once (manifest_repair.go), applies the updates with iceberg-go's builder, patches statistics, name mapping and spec-required keys, stages v{version+1}.metadata.json exclusively (or v{N}-<uuid> when taken) in the table's location (tableLocation: metadata directory, else the assigned warehouse location) and calls UpdateTable with the version token it read. A conflict deletes the staged file and retries from a fresh read, up to three attempts with jittered backoff; the third conflict answers 409 CommitFailedException.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.when: Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE/ALTER from an engine, and the commit that finishes a staged create.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_commit.go.why: Consequence: this is how every write to an Iceberg table becomes visible; losing a commit loses the data it added, and pointing the catalog at a missing file makes the table unreadable. Design: optimistic concurrency — the version token in the record is the compare, and the client's requirements are re-validated on every retry, so a server-side retry is only accepted when the client's assumptions still hold. The metadata file is staged before the pointer flips, so a reader never sees a pointer to a file that does not exist yet. Compatibility: requirement types, update types, the 409/CommitFailedException retry signal and the response shape follow the REST spec.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_metrics.go.character: POST .../tables/{table}/metrics: accepts and discards scan and commit reports
gotchas: The report is not checked against the table: any authenticated caller can post one for any name, and it is dropped either way.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_metrics.go.if_broken: Engines log errors on every query.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_metrics.go.ux: No error noise in engine logs.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_metrics.go.what: handleReportMetrics validates namespace and table, reads at most 1 MiB, requires a report-type field and answers 204. An oversized report is discarded with 204 as well.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_metrics.go.when: After scans and commits by clients that send reports (Java and Spark do by default).
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_metrics.go.why: Consequence: engines report metrics after every scan or commit; a 404 here logs an error per query and some clients treat repeated failures as a broken catalog. Design: no metrics store exists, so the endpoint only satisfies the protocol.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.character: Iceberg namespace operations (config, list, create, get, exists, drop, update properties) translated onto s3tables namespace calls
gotchas: UpdateNamespace replaces the whole property map, and the read and the write are separate calls with no version check, so two concurrent property updates can drop each other's keys (see issue note).
ListNamespaces errors are logged at glog.Infof, not V-gated.
404 decisions rely on matching 'not found' in the error text.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.if_broken: Engines cannot attach, namespaces vanish from listings, or property updates are lost.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.issue_note: UpdateNamespaceProperties loses concurrent updates. It reads the properties with GetNamespace, merges the request into that copy, and writes the whole map back with UpdateNamespace, which replaces the properties and compares only the namespace's CreatedAt. Probe (MemFiler hook): client B's update {b:2} lands between client A's read and A's write; both answer 200, and the final properties are {a:1, location} — b is gone.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.ux: CREATE NAMESPACE / SHOW NAMESPACES / ALTER NAMESPACE SET PROPERTIES work from Spark, Trino and PyIceberg.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.what: handleConfig echoes overrides.prefix and defaults.warehouse=s3://<bucket> when the client passes ?warehouse=. List maps ?parent= to a dotted prefix and pages through ListNamespaces. Create, Get, Exists and Drop call the matching s3tables operation; Get and Create add the default 'location' property. handleUpdateNamespaceProperties rejects a key that is both removed and updated (422), reads the namespace with GetNamespace, merges removals and updates into the properties it read, and writes the merged map back with UpdateNamespace, answering the removed/updated/missing summary.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.when: Catalog attach (/v1/config) and namespace DDL from engines.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_namespace.go.why: Consequence: engines create and inspect namespaces before any table operation, and DuckDB's ATTACH relies on overrides.prefix to reach the right bucket. Design: namespaces are s3tables namespaces, so permissions, existence veiling and delete protection come from s3tables. Compatibility: response shapes, 204 for exists/drop, 409 NamespaceNotEmptyException and the update summary follow the REST spec.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_oauth.go.character: The catalog's OAuth2 token endpoint: client_credentials with S3 access keys and RFC 8693 token exchange, issuing HS256 JWTs signed with a key derived from the credential
gotchas: There is no revocation short of rotating or deleting the access key; a token stays valid until it expires.
Bearer verification does not check the issuer claim (token exchange does), so any HS256 token signed with the derived key is accepted.
ValidateS3Credential compares secrets with != (see the s3api_server.go defect).
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_oauth.go.if_broken: OAuth-only clients cannot connect, tokens expire without refresh, or a leaked token can be chain-refreshed forever.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_oauth.go.ux: Spark/PyIceberg configured with credential=<access>:<secret> get tokens and refresh them transparently.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_oauth.go.what: handleOAuthTokens accepts client_id/client_secret from the form or HTTP Basic (never the query string), validates them with ValidateS3Credential and mints a JWT (issuer seaweedfs-iceberg, claims identity_name and access_key) signed with HMAC-SHA256(accessKey, NUL, secret). The lifetime is ICEBERG_OAUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRY seconds (default 3600, at most a year). handleTokenExchange verifies a subject_token by its signature; an expired one is exchangeable only with client authentication by the same access key, within a grace of twice the TTL clamped to 1-24 h, and an unauthenticated exchange never extends the token beyond its own expiry. authenticateBearerKey verifies a presented token by looking up the access key named in its claims and re-deriving the signing key.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_oauth.go.when: Client start-up and token refresh (POST /v1/oauth/tokens); authenticateBearerKey on every request carrying a Bearer token.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_oauth.go.why: Consequence: most Iceberg engines authenticate only through this flow, so a failure here locks them out; a leak of a long-lived token is a credential leak. Design: tokens are stateless, so no token store is needed, and the key derivation ties a token to one credential, so rotating or deleting the access key revokes all its tokens. The access key is in the derivation so two credentials that share a secret cannot forge each other's tokens. Token exchange exists because Iceberg Java 1.10 refreshes through it. Compatibility: grant_type values, the issued_token_type URN and Cache-Control: no-store follow RFC 6749 / 8693.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.character: Iceberg table operations: list, create (including stage-create), register, load, exists, drop and rename, plus the FileIO config and credential vending returned with table metadata
gotchas: If the stored metadata fails to parse, or a location-only record's file is missing, LoadTable answers 200 with empty placeholder metadata instead of an error.
handleTableExists answers 404 for every error, including access denied and server faults.
The default location falls back to ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE, an env var read per request.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.if_broken: Tables cannot be created or loaded, concurrent creates corrupt each other, or drops delete data that should be kept.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.issue_note: DropTable ignores the REST spec's purgeRequested flag (default false): after DeleteTable it always removes the whole table location (cleanupStaleTableLocation, recursive, with data), so a plain DROP TABLE without PURGE deletes every data and metadata file. Probe (s3tablestest MemFiler, open authenticator): create table, put data/part-00000.parquet, DELETE .../tables/t without purgeRequested → 204, and the data file and the table directory are gone. Re-probed at 7506e5f, after #12475 gave server-picked locations their own <name>-<uuid> directory: the same, also for a client-chosen location, where the purge also removes unrelated objects under it; and S3 Tables DeleteTable alone already removes the table's directory with its data, so honoring the flag also needs a catalog-only delete there. Spark DROP TABLE and PyIceberg drop_table send no purge; Trino always sends purgeRequested=true. DropView does the same for a view's location.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.ux: Tables created by one engine are visible to the others; vended credentials let engines read data without static keys.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.what: handleCreateTable picks the table location: the request's location, else properties.warehouse, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE or the bucket, each followed by <ns>/<name>-<uuid>, so a location the server picks is unique to the table. It builds v1 metadata with iceberg-go (newTableMetadata assigns fresh field ids and the default name mapping), confines the location to the bucket and namespace, and asks GetTable whether the name is taken; an existing table is answered 409 AlreadyExistsException. It then checks the CreateTable permission for that location, and either stages the metadata exclusively under .iceberg_staged/ with a marker (stage-create; a marker that cannot be saved fails the request) or stages v1.metadata.json exclusively with a per-request token (stageOwnedMetadata) and registers it with s3tables CreateTable. A CreateTable that answers with another table's location counts as 'already exists'. After a failed registration the staged file is discarded only when the catalog refused it (registrationRefused); when another create took the name, the directory the server picked is removed and the answer is 409. handleRegisterTable checks the CreateTable permission for the metadata location, reads the client-named metadata file (inline or chunked), parses it and registers it, dropping the stored copy when the request would exceed the manager's size cap. handleLoadTable serves the record's metadata (or the file it points at) at tableLocation (the metadata directory, else the record's warehouseLocation, else the name path) and honours ?snapshots=refs. buildFileIOConfig advertises s3.endpoint, path-style access and the region, and vends table-scoped STS credentials (read-only unless the caller may UpdateTable) when the client asked for them. handleDropTable deletes the record and then removes the whole table location; cleanupStaleTableLocation refuses a path another catalog record claims. handleRenameTable calls RenameTable.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.when: Engine DDL: CREATE TABLE, CTAS, REGISTER, DESCRIBE/SELECT (load), DROP, ALTER TABLE RENAME.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_table.go.why: Consequence: this is the DDL surface every engine uses; a wrong create answer lets two writers believe they own one table, and a drop that touches the wrong path deletes data. Design: s3tables owns the record and its concurrency control; this file owns the metadata files. A location the server picks is <name>-<uuid>, so a renamed table's files never sit under a name another table can take, and a create stages its file exclusively and discards it only after a definite refusal. Credentials are vended per table so engines can read data without a gateway-wide key. Compatibility: stage-create, register, ?snapshots=refs, X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation, the response shapes and the 409 on an existing name follow the REST spec; clients that want CREATE IF NOT EXISTS catch the 409 and load the table.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..character: POST /v1/transactions/commit: multi-table commits — every table validated first, every metadata file staged, then the pointers flipped one by one with best-effort rollback
gotchas: The restore UpdateTable carries no version token, so it overwrites whatever is in the record at that moment, including a commit another writer landed after the flip (see issue note).
There is no per-table retry on conflict, unlike the single-table commit; a transaction of busy tables fails often.
Tables must already exist: assert-create is not handled here.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..if_broken: Some tables of a transaction keep the new state while others do not, or a concurrent writer's commit disappears.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..issue_note: The rollback of a failed multi-table commit restores already-flipped tables with an UpdateTable that carries no version token (buildTableRestoreRequest), so it overwrites whatever the record holds at that moment. A commit another writer lands on one of those tables between the transaction's flip and its rollback is silently reverted. The table whose flip failed also has its staged file deleted even when that failure was ambiguous. Reproduced at b9866bae: a transaction flips t1, another writer commits t1 to v3, the flip of t2 fails, and the rollback puts t1 back at v1; the other writer's commit is gone. flipTablePointer discards the version token the flip returns, so the rollback has nothing to compare.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..ux: Multi-table commits either all apply or are rolled back, except on a crash mid-way.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..what: handleCommitTransaction resolves each table change (prepareTableCommit: GetTable, the UpdateTable permission check, current metadata at tableLocation, requirement validation, updates applied with iceberg-go, statistics and name-mapping patches), stages every new metadata file exclusively, then calls UpdateTable per table with its version token. If a flip fails, the tables already flipped are restored with an UpdateTable carrying their previous location, version and metadata (rollbackTablePointers), and the staged files are deleted except those still referenced by a table whose restore failed (cleanupSafeMetadata). A conflict answers 409 CommitFailedException.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..when: Engines that use the multi-table commit endpoint.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_transaction..why: Consequence: engines use this to commit several tables at once (multi-table writes, some MERGE plans); a partial apply leaves those tables inconsistent with each other. Design: the filer has no multi-entry transaction, so validation is all-or-nothing but the flips are sequential with compensation; the code says so: 'not crash-atomic'. Compatibility: request shape and 204 response follow the REST spec.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.character: Iceberg view operations: list, create, load, exists, drop and rename, stored as s3tables view records with a v1.metadata.json beside them
gotchas: s3tables CreateView answers 200 for a name that already holds a view of the same format. A creator that loses a race after the existence check answers with the winner's view when the metadata locations differ (the default since #12475), but with the same client-supplied location it still writes v1.metadata.json over the winner's file, and if that write fails it drops the winner's view (see issue note).
handleViewExists answers 404 for every error.
Drop always removes the view's location.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.if_broken: Views disappear, or two concurrent creators end up with mismatched metadata.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.issue_note: Two defects, both probed at b9866bae. First, CreateView answers 200 for a view that already exists, with the stored definition and whatever the request asked for: the handler short-circuits on its existence check, and s3tables CreateView answers 200 for an existing view of the same format. The Iceberg REST spec answers 409 AlreadyExistsException, as CreateTable here does, so CREATE VIEW v AS <other query> reports success and leaves the old view. Probe: create v1 as 'select 1', create v1 again as 'select 999' -> 200 with 'select 1'. Second, the loser of a concurrent create can still overwrite the winner's v1.metadata.json when both pass the same location. Since #12475 a view created without a location gets its own <name>-<uuid> directory, so the metadata locations differ and the loser answers with the winner's view. With one client-supplied location they are equal: the loser passes the comparison, writes v1.metadata.json non-exclusively over the winner's file, and on a write failure calls dropView by name, which deletes the winner's view. Probe: B's create lands between A's existence check and A's s3tables CreateView, both with location s3://warehouse/ns/v1 -> A answers 200 with 'select 1', LoadView serves 'select 2' from the record and the file holds 'select 1'. See also the s3tables/ note: the record itself can be replaced by a racing create.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.ux: Views created in one engine are visible in the others.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.what: handleCreateView resolves the location (request, properties.warehouse, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE or, by default, s3://<bucket>/<ns>/<view>-<uuid>, a directory of its own), confines it to the bucket, builds view metadata with iceberg-go and answers 200 with the existing definition when the view already exists. Otherwise it registers the view with s3tables CreateView first; when the answer names another metadata location, another create won and its view is returned. Then it writes v1.metadata.json (non-exclusive); if that write fails it drops the view by name. Load serves the record's stored metadata (FullMetadata is required). Drop deletes the record and then removes the whole view location. Rename calls RenameView.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.when: CREATE VIEW / DROP VIEW / ALTER VIEW RENAME and view resolution in engines.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view.go.why: Consequence: SQL views shared between engines (Spark, Trino) live here; losing one breaks every query built on it. Design: unlike tables, the record is written before the file, so a missing namespace or a taken name fails before anything is stored. Views are always served from the record's copy, so the file matters only to readers that open it directly.

weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view_update..character: POST .../views/{view}: the view commit — requirements, updates, a new metadata file and a version-token pointer flip, retried on conflict
gotchas: Every non-conflict error answers 500, including access-denied and not-found answers from UpdateView.
There is no request-size fitting as for tables, so a very large view definition is refused by the manager's size cap.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view_update..if_broken: View changes are lost or fail with 500.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view_update..ux: Concurrent view replacements retry instead of overwriting each other.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view_update..what: handleUpdateView reads the view, checks the UpdateView permission, validates requirements against the stored metadata, applies the updates with iceberg-go's view builder, stages v{N+1}.metadata.json exclusively (stageCommitMetadata) and calls UpdateView with the version token. A conflict deletes the staged file and retries up to three times; any other failure deletes the staged file and answers 500.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view_update..when: View replacement and property changes from engines.
weed/s3api/iceberg/handlers_view_update..why: Consequence: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW and ALTER VIEW land here; a lost update silently reverts a view definition. Design: the same optimistic-concurrency loop as the table commit, with the record's version token as the compare.

weed/s3api/iceberg/iceberg.go.character: Package doc file of the Iceberg REST catalog: no code, only the statement that the package implements the Iceberg REST Catalog spec on top of S3 Tables metadata
gotchas: The AST extracts no symbols from this file, so the node has no edges; that is expected.
weed/s3api/iceberg/iceberg.go.if_broken: Nothing breaks; the package loses its doc comment.
weed/s3api/iceberg/iceberg.go.what: Declares package iceberg with its doc comment. Every symbol of the package lives in the other files of lane 8.
weed/s3api/iceberg/iceberg.go.why: Consequence: none at runtime; it only carries the package documentation shown by go doc. Design: the catalog is a protocol adapter, not a store: every namespace and table record lives in the s3tables catalog, and this package translates Iceberg REST requests into s3tables operations plus metadata files on the filer.

weed/s3api/iceberg/manifest_repair.go.character: Commit-time repair of foreign manifests: adds the spec's avro field-id annotations and absolutizes bucket-relative paths, so snapshots written by lax engines are readable by the others
gotchas: A manifest with a genuine avro map field, or any field outside the spec's known ids, is left unrepaired rather than half-annotated.
The originals stay in place next to the repaired- copies; nothing deletes them.
weed/s3api/iceberg/manifest_repair.go.if_broken: Snapshots from lax writers are unreadable elsewhere, or a repair rewrites a manifest wrongly.
weed/s3api/iceberg/manifest_repair.go.ux: Tables written by ClickHouse can be queried from other engines.
weed/s3api/iceberg/manifest_repair.go.what: For each add-snapshot update whose manifest list sits in the table's metadata directory, repairManifestList loads the list and, when it lacks field-id annotations or uses relative paths, transcodes it and every manifest it references (annotateAvroRecordFields with the v2 manifest_file / manifest_entry ids, partition ids from the manifest's embedded partition-spec, absolute data file paths, OCF 'content' and 'partition-spec-id' metadata fixed to agree with the list). The repaired copies are saved as repaired-<name> beside the originals and the snapshot is pointed at them. loadTableMetadataBlob reads metadata-directory files inline or, for files uploaded through the S3 gateway, by streaming their chunks (at most 64 MiB). Any failure keeps the original update.
weed/s3api/iceberg/manifest_repair.go.when: Once per commit request that adds a snapshot (table commits and create-on-commit).
weed/s3api/iceberg/manifest_repair.go.why: Consequence: ClickHouse's experimental Iceberg writes (among others) produce manifests without field ids and with bucket-relative paths; Spark, Trino and PyIceberg then cannot read those snapshots although the data is fine. Design: the catalog is the one chokepoint every commit passes through, so the repair happens there once, best effort, and never fails a commit. Repair is confined to direct children of the metadata directory so it never reads or writes elsewhere.

weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_compliance.g.character: Backfills the five spec-required table-metadata keys that iceberg-go drops when empty, without reordering the document
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_compliance.g.if_broken: Empty tables fail to load in strict clients.
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_compliance.g.ux: Freshly created tables open in Spark, Trino and Java clients.
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_compliance.g.what: ensureMetadataSpecCompliance adds current-snapshot-id (-1), snapshots, snapshot-log, metadata-log ([]) and refs ({}) when absent, by splicing them before the closing brace so key order is preserved. When one is an explicit JSON null it falls back to a map re-marshal that replaces the nulls. Unparsable input is returned unchanged.
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_compliance.g.when: Create, commit and every load/commit response (types.go MarshalJSON).
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_compliance.g.why: Consequence: strict clients fail to parse metadata of tables with no snapshots ('Cannot parse missing long current-snapshot-id'). Design: byte-level splicing keeps iceberg-go's declared key order and produces deterministic output; the slower re-marshal path exists only for nulls, which iceberg-go never emits itself.

weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_files.go.character: Reads and writes the v*.metadata.json files on the filer, inline in the entry, and resolves the metadata a table currently serves
gotchas: deleteMetadataFile deletes by name with no token; the table commit, view update and transaction paths still clean up with it (see the defect on handlers_commit.go), while the create paths use deleteStagedMetadataFile.
A metadata file that is missing reads as 'no metadata', not as an error, so the caller substitutes placeholder metadata.
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_files.go.if_broken: Commits overwrite one another's metadata, a cleanup deletes another request's file, loads fail, or a table falls back to placeholder metadata.
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_files.go.ux: Engines that read metadata-location from storage see the same metadata the catalog returns.
weed/s3api/iceberg/metadata_files.go.what: saveMetadataBlob creates missing directories (bucket, each table-path segment, metadata/) and writes the file as one filer entry whose Content holds the bytes and whose extended attributes carry the mime type and any caller attributes (the stage token), with OExcl when exclusive is set; an existing name then answers filer_pb.ErrEntryAlreadyExists. deleteStagedMetadataFile removes a staged file only while it still carries the request's stage token, an ExpectedExtended precondition the filer checks under the path lock, and answers errStagedFileReplaced otherwise. deleteMetadataFile removes a file by name; loadMetadataFile returns an inline entry's content. currentMetadataBytes returns the metadata a table serves: the copy stored in the catalog record (FullMetadata) or, for a record that keeps only a location, the file at that location (via loadTableMetadataBlob, confined to the bucket). It returns nil when the record has neither or the file is missing.
